body:
No job in this project should run on GitHub-hosted runners any more. The macOS suites already run on this project's own Macs (`macos.yml`, macOS 15 and the newest macOS). The GitHub copies and the CI job that waited on them can go.

- `macos.yml` becomes the macOS gate. Its two jobs become required checks on `main`, replacing `CI / macos`, and the release workflows check it on the commit they cut from.
- Delete the GitHub CI workflows: `ci-pr.yml`, `ci-macos.yml`, `formula-macos.yml` and `retry-infra-failures.yml` and `hassfest.yml` (`ci.yml` already runs hassfest and HACS).
- Re-vendor the standard from the release that retires the GitHub-runner helpers.
- Update the docs and invariant tests that describe the GitHub side.

The release-side GitHub workflows (the `.pkg`, bottles, arm64 and install-matrix legs) move in a separate change.
title: Run CI on this project's own runners only

body:
Every release asset is still built or tested on GitHub-hosted runners: the signed `.pkg`, the Homebrew bottles, the arm64 Linux set and the macOS and arm64 install legs. This project now has its own macOS 15, newest-macOS and arm64 runners, so all of that can move in-house and GitHub only receives the release.

- `release-macos.yml` and `bottles.yml` move to `.forgejo/workflows/`. The `.pkg` is built, signed, notarized and stapled on the macOS 15 VM and tested again on the newest-macOS VM. Bottles are built for macOS 15, Linux amd64 and Linux arm64. Each workflow uploads to all three releases (public Forgejo, NAS, GitHub).
- `release-arm64.yml` becomes the arm64 publisher. Its compare-with-GitHub shadow goes, and so does `.github/workflows/release-linux-arm64.yml`.
- `install-matrix.yml` covers Linux amd64, Linux arm64 and macOS in one run. `install-matrix-arm64.yml` and the GitHub install matrix go, along with `publish.yml`'s GitHub dispatch.
- The NAS bridge jobs (`nas-bridge`, `nas-bottles`) go, because every producer reaches the NAS directly. `reconcile` waits for the `.pkg` and the arm64 set before healing.
- The Apple signing secrets move to Forgejo org secrets.

Follows the CI-side change in #178.

body:
Closes #179

Large diff: moving four release workflows from `.github` to `.forgejo` (or merging them in), plus the tests and docs that pin them, can't be split without leaving a release path half on GitHub.

## What changes
- `release-macos.yml` and `bottles.yml` move to Forgejo. The `.pkg` is built, signed, notarized and stapled on macos-15-vm, then tested on macos-27-vm. Bottles build on ubuntu-latest, ubuntu-26.04-arm and macos-15-vm. Each uploads straight to the Forgejo, NAS and GitHub releases. The nas-pkg and nas-bottles bridges are gone.
- `release-arm64.yml` is now the real arm64 publisher. `release-linux-arm64.yml`, the shadow and `compare-arch-build.sh` are deleted.
- One `install-matrix.yml` covers amd64, arm64 and both macOS VMs (pkg/spctl, bottle pour, uvx). The GitHub install matrix, `install-matrix-arm64.yml` and the GitHub dispatch are deleted.
- reconcile waits until the .pkg and arm64 set are on both the public Forgejo and the NAS.
- The stable-cut refusal step and its test are removed. `.github/workflows` is empty, and a test keeps it that way.
- Deviation, already approved: the .pkg and bottles stay as their own workflows instead of being folded into publish.yml.
- All eight `MACOS_*` secrets are present as Forgejo org secrets.

## Proof (private proof repo; build and verify only, no uploads)
- Bottles: all three legs. Keg lists and tabs are identical to the GitHub-built bottles (tab differences are only Homebrew version drift).
- Unsigned .pkg: payload files and per-binary minimum macOS are identical to the GitHub-built .pkg.
- macOS install legs on macos-15-vm and macos-27-vm: spctl accepts the published pkg as notarized, the bottle pours and uvx works, on two runs back to back.
- Signed .pkg, run 37953 (2 jobs): built, signed, notarized (Accepted) and stapled on macos-15-vm twice in a row. `stapler validate` OK, `spctl -a -t install` accepted as Notarized Developer ID, payload files IDENTICAL to the GitHub-built pkg (5 entries), and minimum macOS per binary IDENTICAL.

- Signing needed one change on the runner side: each job now sets the keychain search list and default (`list-keychains -d user -s`, `default-keychain -d user -s`), since every job starts with neither. A test pins both lines.

## Checks
ruff, mypy, pytest with coverage floors, shellcheck, actionlint and doc links all pass locally. Codex review found nothing.

##### v8 - What's new

> \[!IMPORTANT]
> actions/download-artifact\@​v8 has been migrated to an ESM module. This should be transparent to the caller but forks might need to make significant changes.

> \[!IMPORTANT]
> Hash mismatches will now error by default. Users can override this behavior with a setting change (see below).

##### Direct downloads

To support direct uploads in `actions/upload-artifact`, the action will no longer attempt to unzip all downloaded files. Instead, the action checks the `Content-Type` header ahead of unzipping and skips non-zipped files. Callers wishing to download a zipped file as-is can also set the new `skip-decompress` parameter to `true`.

##### Enforced checks (breaking)

A previous release introduced digest checks on the download. If a download hash didn't match the expected hash from the server, the action would log a warning. Callers can now configure the behavior on mismatch with the `digest-mismatch` parameter. To be secure by default, we are now defaulting the behavior to `error` which will fail the workflow run.

##### ESM

To support new versions of the @​actions/\* packages, we've upgraded the package to ESM.

##### What's Changed

- Don't attempt to un-zip non-zipped downloads by [@​danwkennedy](https://github.com/danwkennedy) in [#​460](https://github.com/actions/download-artifact/pull/460)
- Add a setting to specify what to do on hash mismatch and default it to `error` by [@​danwkennedy](https://github.com/danwkennedy) in [#​461](https://github.com/actions/download-artifact/pull/461)

##### What's Changed

- Update README.md by [@​nebuk89](https://github.com/nebuk89) in [#​407](https://github.com/actions/download-artifact/pull/407)
- BREAKING fix: inconsistent path behavior for single artifact downloads by ID by [@​GrantBirki](https://github.com/GrantBirki) in [#​416](https://github.com/actions/download-artifact/pull/416)

##### v5.0.0

##### 🚨 Breaking Change

This release fixes an inconsistency in path behavior for single artifact downloads by ID. **If you're downloading single artifacts by ID, the output path may change.**

##### What Changed

Previously, **single artifact downloads** behaved differently depending on how you specified the artifact:

- **By name**: `name: my-artifact` → extracted to `path/` (direct)
- **By ID**: `artifact-ids: 12345` → extracted to `path/my-artifact/` (nested)

Now both methods are consistent:

- **By name**: `name: my-artifact` → extracted to `path/` (unchanged)
- **By ID**: `artifact-ids: 12345` → extracted to `path/` (fixed - now direct)

##### Migration Guide

##### ✅ No Action Needed If:

- You download artifacts by **name**
- You download **multiple** artifacts by ID
- You already use `merge-multiple: true` as a workaround

##### ⚠️ Action Required If:

You download **single artifacts by ID** and your workflows expect the nested directory structure.

**Before v5 (nested structure):**

```yaml
- uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
  with:
    artifact-ids: 12345
    path: dist

# Files were in: dist/my-artifact/
```

> Where `my-artifact` is the name of the artifact you previously uploaded

**To maintain old behavior (if needed):**

```yaml
- uses: actions/download-artifact@v5
  with:
    artifact-ids: 12345
    path: dist/my-artifact  # Explicitly specify the nested path
```

##### What's Changed

The release of upload-artifact\@​v4 and download-artifact\@​v4 are major changes to the backend architecture of Artifacts. They have numerous performance and behavioral improvements.

ℹ️ However, this is a major update that includes breaking changes. Artifacts created with versions v3 and below are not compatible with the v4 actions. Uploads and downloads *must* use the same major actions versions. There are also key differences from previous versions that may require updates to your workflows.

For more information, please see:

1. The [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2023-12-14-github-actions-artifacts-v4-is-now-generally-available/) post.
2. The [migration documentation](https://github.com/actions/upload-artifact/blob/main/docs/MIGRATION.md).
3. As well as the underlying npm package, [@​actions/artifact](https://github.com/actions/toolkit/tree/main/packages/artifact) documentation.

##### Breaking Changes

1. download-artifact\@​v4+ is not currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) yet. If you are on GHES, you must use [v3](https://github.com/actions/download-artifact/releases/tag/v3) (Node 16) or [v3-node20](https://github.com/actions/download-artifact/releases/tag/v3-node20) (Node 20).
2. On self hosted runners, additional [firewall rules](https://github.com/actions/toolkit/tree/main/packages/artifact#breaking-changes) may be required.
3. Downloading artifacts that were created from `action/upload-artifact@v3` and below are not supported.

For assistance with breaking changes, see [MIGRATION.md](https://github.com/actions/upload-artifact/blob/main/docs/MIGRATION.md).

##### Improvements

1. Downloads are significantly faster, upwards of 90% improvement in worst case scenarios.
2. Artifacts can be downloaded from other workflow runs and repositories when supplied with a PAT.

##### v7 What's new

##### Direct Uploads

Adds support for uploading single files directly (unzipped). Callers can set the new `archive` parameter to `false` to skip zipping the file during upload. Right now, we only support single files. The action will fail if the glob passed resolves to multiple files. The `name` parameter is also ignored with this setting. Instead, the name of the artifact will be the name of the uploaded file.

##### ESM

To support new versions of the `@actions/*` packages, we've upgraded the package to ESM.

body:
Refs #185.

Moved from https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/pull/14, opened by Stephan Garland (@stephanGarland on GitHub) on 2026-11-06, with his commits unchanged. **Not yet reviewed.** Sent as an AGit pull request so CI does not run unreviewed code; a maintainer re-opens it from a branch after review.

---

I split this work into three separate PRs as I wasn't sure if you'd want the bridge and broker.

## What and why

The EVO provisions over the same BLE protocomm channel as the LR4 and uses the same MQTT envelope, but its register map is banked and different, so the LR4 driver can't talk to it. This PR adds it in two commits, which can be reviewed (or merged) separately: the library first, then the integration.

**Library** (`devices/litter_robot_evo/`, laid out like `litter_robot_4`)
- **Provisioning:** BLE now accepts the EVO's service UUID, name and `LRE-…` serial (on the EVO the long hyphenated label line is the serial). EVOs get their native `prod/robots/<serial>/…` topics; LR4 provisioning is unchanged.
- **Protocol:** commands are `0xTTBBRRVVVV` (read or write, bank, register, value). A single message can read every readable register, and the robot answers in one reply.
- **Commands:** separate screen and status-LED brightness, cycle delay, lockout, sleep schedule, the robot's clock, clean and empty cycles, change filter, drawer-level reset, power on/off. EVO commands are classified separately in `safety.py`, so LR4 behavior doesn't change.
- **Also:** a `whiskerless evo` CLI subcommand and `docs/devices/litter-robot-evo/protocol.md`, with each fact marked proven, inferred or open.

**Integration**
- **Discovery and state:** EVOs are discovered on `prod/robots/<serial>/…`. The integration reads the robot's state at startup, on reconnect and after power-on, and sets the robot's clock each time, so its sleep schedule keeps correct time even without the cloud.
- **Panel light:** the Whisker app only offers Low/Medium/High, which set the screen and status LED together. Here they're two separate sliders (1–100), plus a preset with an **Off** option that drops both to 1.
- **Other entities:** cycle delay, control lock, Sleep mode and its times, the cycle and maintenance buttons, power, status, pet weight, cycle counts, and drawer and bonnet sensors.
- **Blueprint:** keeps chosen night and day levels across a time window and puts them back after the robot reconnects (the Whisker cloud resends the app's preset when that happens). It never overrides a change made by hand.

The integration's library pin still needs a release that includes the driver.

Tested on a real EVO (robot firmware v4.7.0, IoT firmware v2.6.4):
- provisioned with this branch and discovered by the integration;
- every command marked proven was sent and checked against the robot's echo;
- after an HA restart every entity filled in by itself;
- a night boundary set the night level.

Not done yet: remote reset, sending a paused empty cycle home without a panel press, cloud-free pet identification, and the weight-sensor scale.

## Sibling repo

- [ ] Ported to the sibling repo (link the PR)
- [x] Not applicable, because: Whisker-specific device support.
- [ ] Deliberate variance, recorded in `VARIANCE.md`

## Checks

- [x] Regression test that fails on the parent commit
- [x] `STANDARD.lock` still in sync (no vendored file edited in place)

- **Library:** 1634 tests pass at 99.28% coverage, with `safety.py` and the EVO modules at 100%.
- **Integration:** the suite passes at 99.81%, with `config_flow.py` at 100% and LR4 snapshots unchanged.
- **Lint and types:** ruff and mypy are clean.

EVO support also depends on #218. It will make unknown LR4 command types require `allow_dangerous`, so EVO and LR4 can ship with the same safety rule.
EVO support also depends on #219. LR4 and EVO should both allow verified setting values by default and require `allow_dangerous` for unverified values. Each model will use its own verified ranges.

Thanks for the EVO work, @stephanGarland. Let’s plan to start with an opt-in preview from a whiskerless branch after #217, #218, and #219 land. I can split the patch into PRs for Bluetooth setup, the driver and command safety, Home Assistant, and the optional blueprint and examples while preserving your authorship.

The preview would start with Power off disabled. Unknown command types and unverified setting values would require `allow_dangerous`, and the docs and tests would use a clearly labeled synthetic serial.

The preview would need to be tested on a real EVO. I don’t own one, so I’d be relying on your help with that. Shared setup changes would also need an LR4 bench test. Listing EVO as community-supported would require a named EVO owner who can help reproduce bugs and test future changes.

body:
Refs #186.

Moved from https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/pull/15, opened by Stephan Garland (@stephanGarland on GitHub) on 2026-11-06, with his commits unchanged. **Not yet reviewed.** Sent as an AGit pull request so CI does not run unreviewed code; a maintainer re-opens it from a branch after review.

---

I split this work into three separate PRs as I wasn't sure if you'd want the bridge and broker.

## What and why

Taking a robot off Whisker's cloud also takes away the Whisker app. With this bridge you can keep both. The robot stays on your local broker, and the bridge connects to Whisker's AWS IoT endpoint as the robot, relaying messages unchanged in both directions. The app keeps working, and every command the cloud sends is visible locally, which makes working out new commands much easier. It's inspired by [rethink](https://github.com/anszom/rethink)'s bridge mode; no rethink code is used.

- **Library:** `whiskerless.bridge` works with any model; the local and cloud topic prefixes are configurable.
- **Home Assistant:** a Cloud bridge entry with an on/off switch, a connection sensor, a traffic event (so messages show up in the logbook) and a send-message action. There's an example dashboard in `examples/cloud-bridge/`.
- **Getting the robot's identity:** the Whisker app writes the robot's certificate and key over BLE during setup. `docs/setup/cloud-bridge.md` explains how to capture that on iOS or Android, and `scripts/cloud_identity.py` pulls the certificate and key out of the capture.
- Messages you send toward the robot go through `safety.py`; traffic relayed from the cloud passes through untouched.

Tested on a real EVO: with the bridge running, the app stayed fully usable and every app action showed up on the local broker.

Possible follow-up: the app gets that certificate and key from Whisker's API. If whiskerless could fetch it with the user's login, the BLE capture wouldn't be needed.

## Sibling repo

- [ ] Ported to the sibling repo (link the PR)
- [x] Not applicable, because: it relays to Whisker's cloud specifically.
- [ ] Deliberate variance, recorded in `VARIANCE.md`

## Checks

- [x] Regression test that fails on the parent commit
- [x] `STANDARD.lock` still in sync (no vendored file edited in place)

The library suite passes at 99.19% and the integration suite at 99.78%, with `safety.py` and `config_flow.py` at 100%.

body:
Refs #187.

Moved from https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/pull/16, opened by Stephan Garland (@stephanGarland on GitHub) on 2026-11-06, with his commits unchanged. **Not yet reviewed.** Sent as an AGit pull request so CI does not run unreviewed code; a maintainer re-opens it from a branch after review.

---

I split this work into three separate PRs as I wasn't sure if you'd want the bridge and broker.

## What and why

The robot connects to its broker on port 8883 without a username or password. Home Assistant OS's Mosquitto add-on requires both, so on HAOS the robot can't use it, even though the README currently suggests it can.

This adds an optional **Whiskerless robot broker** add-on (this repo also becomes an add-on repository; HACS is unaffected). It's a small Mosquitto with a TLS listener for the robot, and it bridges the robot's topics into the Mosquitto add-on, so the integration sees them as usual.

`docs/setup/robot-broker.md` covers when you need it and when you don't. It also covers what to do when something else already uses port 8883: the robot's port can't be changed, so you redirect its traffic with a NAT rule on your router. The robot then needs a fixed IP, since the rule matches on it.

Tested on a real EVO on a separate VLAN, with another service holding port 8883 on the host.

## Sibling repo

- [ ] Ported to the sibling repo (link the PR)
- [x] Not applicable, because: Valetudo can log in with a username and password, so it can use the Mosquitto add-on directly.
- [ ] Deliberate variance, recorded in `VARIANCE.md`

comments.body: _@b12e on GitHub, 2026-11-09:_ > Home Assistant OS's Mosquitto add-on requires both, so on HAOS the robot can't use it, even though the README currently suggests it can. No, it doesn't. But you need to change some config. I'm running the Mosquitto's add-on on HAOS for all other MQTT things and the Litter Robot is publishing to the very same broker without issue. in the Mosquitto addon settings in HA -> Settings -> Apps -> Mosquitto -> Config via UI: or as YAML: ```yaml customize: active: true folder: mosquitto ``` And then a new file (modify to your own needs) in `/share/mosquitto/` (can access via SSH or via the VS Code addon) (I named it `whiskerless.conf`): ```nginx listener 8883 protocol mqtt cafile /ssl/whiskerless/ca.crt certfile /ssl/whiskerless/server.crt keyfile /ssl/whiskerless/server.key require_certificate true use_identity_as_username true ``` Remember to point to the correct path for your certs.

Thanks for testing this on an EVO with another service already using port 8883, @stephanGarland. The HAOS guide was missing the custom listener that b12e described. With #230 merged, `whiskerless setup` on `main` generates the listener file, and the guide shows how to enable it in the official Mosquitto app.

That setup still needs port 8883 free at the broker address. The redirect in this PR handles that conflict on the same host. I’m closing this PR to keep the supported HAOS setup to one broker.

https://forgejo.bryantserver.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/src/branch/main/docs/setup/mqtt-broker.md#user-content-use-the-official-mosquitto-broker-app

title: fix(lr4): firmware-aware decoding for ESP 1.4.x (status enums, is_cleaning, litter suppression, pic_firmware)

body:
_Recreated from GitHub pull request [#3](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/pull/3), opened by @CryingPecan on 2026-07-28, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

_This is a record of the pull request, not the pull request itself: its commits are kept in the maintainer's archive and were not pushed here._

---

Companion to #2 (independent — merges either order). This one unlocks the data that never reaches the state document: the coordinator previously used activity messages purely as a poll trigger and discarded their contents, but on a real robot three families of facts live *only* there.

**Pet weight works — it was just being thrown away.** Register 0x09 fires once per cat visit (int16/100 lb). 42 h of capture on my hopper-equipped LR4 (ESP 1.4.4): 21 readings, 17 visits, two clearly distinguishable cats (4.2–4.8 lb and 7.2–9.0 lb). The local state doc has no weight field at all, so `cat_weight` was permanently null before this.

**New register: 0x57 = hopper link.** Not in the register map. `0xFFF1` (-15) = link lost — live-proven by detaching the hopper, and it also fires on any bonnet movement (the hopper mounts on the back of the bonnet). Positive values (19/30/35–48) form a per-visit choreography whose middle value loosely tracks the measured cat weight — semantics open, so only the connected/disconnected distinction is decoded; raw passes through.

**Hopper dispense (0x0C) observed in the wild** — your `LITTER_HOPPER_DISPENSED` constant is real: a phase-tagged burst (`0x010A`/`0x1059`/`0x2078`-style) at the clean-cycle tail, 3 dispenses captured, litter restored to target each time. Raw values pass through undecoded until the phases are pinned.

Ships: `events.py` in the library (typed events, defensive extraction — unknown registers can never break it), coordinator folding events into `WhiskerlessData`, and three new entities (Last cat visit, Last hopper dispense, Hopper connected) plus Pet weight now actually populating. Activity-derived values are unknown after an HA restart until the next event — restore-on-restart deliberately left out to keep this reviewable; happy to follow up with it.

5 new library tests with fixtures copied verbatim from the captures.

Pushed two more activity-only registers to this PR, both live-proven on the production 1.4.4 robot during owner-narrated sessions:

- **0xBC = visit duration (seconds of settled weight)**, firing once at visit end. Proven against narrated visits: three deliberate ~5 s cat placements all reported 0 (and produced no 0x09), natural visits report 9-21 s. It's also the gate for the weight event — ~9 s+ always weighed, an owner-witnessed 8 s visit did not. A panel Reset press emits an unrelated large value (592) on the same register, so extraction caps plausible durations at 300 s. New 'Last visit duration' sensor; a duration event also stamps last_cat_visit, so hop-throughs too short to weigh still register as visits.
- **0x56 = waste-drawer bay events**: completely silent across 6 days of continuous capture until the drawer physically moved during a narrated bag change — 10 on pull-out, 14 on re-insert (flagged single-session evidence in the code; unknown codes pass through undecoded). New 'Waste drawer removed' binary sensor — a capability the cloud integration doesn't offer.

Both documented in const.py with the capture evidence.

_@CryingPecan on GitHub, 2026-08-06:_

Field correction to the drawer-bay decode, courtesy of a second narrated drawer pull 5 days after the first: **removal is consistently 10 (2/2), but the re-insert code VARIES** — 14 the first time, 28 the second — and 12 fires occasionally with the drawer seated. The original two-code decode latched the binary sensor at 'removed' when the unseen insert code arrived (observed live in production). Pushed a fix: 10 = removed, any other 0x56 value = seated — self-healing for future unknown codes.

Bonus finding from the same period (in const docs on the decode PR): the DFI cycle counter self-resets when the firmware *detects* a drawer empty — 0x42/0x45/0x46 zeroed on the first post-empty cycle whose dump-phase measurement confirmed the drop, seen on both bag changes.

_@CryingPecan on GitHub, 2026-08-07:_

One more addition, and it's a first-of-its-kind entity: **the hopper's fill gauge, decoded from dispense phase 1** (an 11-day capture happened to span a full hopper drain). The dispense triple's phases: 0 and 2 are invariant step markers (266/271/276, 120-121), but phase 1 tracked the hopper's contents — 89-92 while maintained near the owner's ~90% litter target all week, then declining monotonically (76, 70, 69, 68, 67, 66) as the hopper visibly ran down. It also retroactively explains the 87 we captured at hopper reattach during provisioning week.

New `Hopper fill (raw)` sensor — deliberately unitless: the true-empty and refill anchors are imminent on the production robot (owner is letting it run dry on purpose) and will calibrate a scale in a follow-up. Note the Whisker cloud offers NO hopper level at all (hopperStatus is just ENABLED/DISABLED), so this is a genuinely new capability, not parity.

_@CryingPecan on GitHub, 2026-08-08:_

The drain-to-refill arc completed live tonight, calibrating the fill gauge end to end — and yielding a **'Hopper out of litter' binary sensor** (pushed):

- 89-92 while maintained near target (weeks of baseline)
- monotonic decline while draining: 76 → 70 → 69 → 68 → 67 → 66
- **flatline at 66-70 with the hopper visually empty all day** — the floor reading of the bare auger. Crucially, the firmware NEVER flags empty: it ran a full, normal 3-phase dispense after every single cycle (5/5 that day), delivering nothing. Dispense frequency pinning at every-cycle is the behavioral corroborator.
- **immediate jump to 84 on the first post-refill dispense** (owner-narrated refill; fresh litter mounds unevenly, so a fresh pour reads slightly below the settled 89-92 band)

The empty and supplied bands don't overlap; the sensor uses <= 72. Neither the cloud integration nor the Whisker app offers any hopper-level or hopper-empty signal — the LR4's hopper has been silently measuring itself all along and nobody surfaced it.

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-09:_

Merged into `main` on the Forgejo source of truth (this mirror is read-only, so GitHub can't auto-close it). Your commits are preserved with you as author; the Claude Code trailers were stripped during the rebase, and the multi-paragraph bodies became single-line subjects to match the repo's commit convention. The rationale from your PR descriptions has been folded into the docs and CHANGELOG instead.

Shipping in 0.2.0. I'll send you a longer write-up separately — your work turned up something significant about our own `robotStatus` map that changed what we merged.

Smallest of the series (independent of #2/#3). Your library already ships `set_panel_brightness()` and its wire test — but nothing decoded the read side and no entity exposed it. Live ESP 1.4.4 state docs carry `DisplayIntensityHigh`/`DisplayIntensityLow` as plain ints (my robot reports 40/50), so this just closes the loop:

- models: decode the two fields
- coordinator: `async_set_panel_brightness` with read-back verify of both bytes
- number platform: two CONFIG sliders — *Panel brightness (active)* and *(dimmed)*. A write composes the packed 0x0E value from the changed slider plus the current sibling byte, and refuses (with a clear error) until a state doc has reported current values, so we never blind-write half the register.

Write path not yet exercised on my robot — happy to run it live before you merge if you want a PROVEN tag on the round-trip; the encoding itself is your existing PROVEN 0x0E entry.

comments.body:
_@CryingPecan on GitHub, 2026-07-28:_

Write path now live-PROVEN on the ESP 1.4.4 robot: dimmed 50 → 45 → 50 via the new slider, each write committed and read back through the 0x0E verify, and the packed write left the active byte untouched (stayed 40) — no half-register clobbering. Running this build in production now.

**Labels question closed — behaviorally proven, two observations on the live 1.4.4 robot:**

So High/Low name the *ambient* light level, not the brightness rank — and the stock configuration is deliberately brighter at night (40 day / 50 night), which is why the field names looked swapped. title: feat(lr4): expose panel display brightness (register 0x0E) in Home Assistant

body:
_Recreated from GitHub issue [#5](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/issues/5), opened by @CryingPecan on 2026-08-08, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

---

From 12 days of continuous capture on a production ESP 1.4.4 robot (full context in the field report + PRs #2/#3):

**Register 0x01 fires on physical panel button presses and at no other time.** Labeled ground truth:

- Cycle press → `0x010201` (3 samples: guided session 07-26, owner resume 07-31, post-refill 08-07)
- Reset press → `0x010401` (4 samples: guided session 07-26, drawer session 08-01, plus two more narrated presses)

Pattern reads as `(button_id << 8) | press_type` with 0x01 = short press. Cycle = 0x02, Reset = 0x04 — bit-flag spacing suggests Power/Empty/Connect occupy 0x01/0x08/0x10 (unverified; owner hasn't pressed those yet).

**Why it matters:** if 0x01 accepts type-2 *writes*, it may synthesize panel presses — which would recover the missing actions (cycle trigger, reset/tare) that the recovered firmware never exposed as opcodes. That's an untraced write, so it's firmly behind the safety guard until designed as a careful opt-in experiment — but it's the best lead the capture has produced. Our robot is available as the testbed if you want to design that experiment together.

comments.body:
_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-12:_

Confirmed. `0x01` takes type-2 writes, and the bit-flag spacing holds: Empty is `0x010801`, Power is `0x010101`.

`0x02010201` runs a clean cycle, `0x02010401` presses Reset. Both proven on 1.1.75 across several trials, register echoing the value back each time. They ship as HA buttons now, Empty and Power disabled by default since Power takes the robot off the network and nothing over MQTT brings it back.

One thing that does not work: only press type `01` can be synthesised. Writing type `02` (the 3 second hold) produces no event at all, so the filter wizard and every other hold-only chord is unreachable this way. Whisker's own cloud has no long press either.

Closing since the question is answered.

title: Protocol finding: register 0x01 = panel button event reports (a lead on the missing actions)

body:
_Recreated from GitHub issue [#6](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/issues/6), opened by @CryingPecan on 2026-08-08, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

---

Across 12 days of capture, a family of values appears on *two different* status registers' activity events:

- `0x34` (robotStatus) emitted 0x1064 (×35+), 0x2064, 0x1065
- `0x4F` (robotCycleState) emitted 0x1064, 0x2065

Identical values on different registers strongly suggests these activity events are not plain `(reg << 16) | val16` — a second encode path (phase-tagged? flag-carrying?) seems to exist. They fire at cycle start/end boundaries.

Related timing decode (semantics known, encoding not): **`0x34 = 0x02C0` fires every ~2 minutes during the clean-cycle WAIT countdown** — verified against every wait period in the capture (90+ samples). It's a countdown tick, but 0x02C0 doesn't fit any status enum.

Raw captures available for all of these.

comments.body:
_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-12:_

Confirmed on two 1.1.75 robots, and it is a bit worse than a second encoding.

Over 50 hours, 67 of 208 deduped `0x34` emissions are not `robotStatus` enum members: the `0x_064`/`0x_065` family plus `0x02C0`. `0x4F` has five values outside its enum too, all on one robot, all in interrupted cycles. Anything decoding activity `0x34` through the status enum is producing garbage for a third of it.

The `0x02C0` tick reads exactly as described. Three ticks two minutes apart, stopping 13 seconds before a cycle that fired one second off `cleanCycleWaitTime`. It is the clean-delay countdown.

Encoding itself still open.

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-16:_

The `0x02C0` half has a window now, and the `0x10xx`/`0xE065` half has a trigger. The
encoding is still open, but both shapes are narrower than they were.

**`0x3402C0` fires only between a visit ending and a clean cycle starting.** All twelve
ticks in a 23h37m capture sit inside one of four windows, two minutes apart to within a
second, and none stray:

| cycle at | ticks |
|---|---|
| 16:36:49 | 16:32:30, 16:34:30, 16:36:31 |
| 20:49:38 | 20:43:18, 20:45:18, 20:47:19, 20:49:19 |
| 23:48:34 | 23:45:03, 23:47:03 |
| 02:14:32 | 02:09:30, 02:11:31, 02:13:31 |

The sixth cycle — the one released by waking, not by the timer — got no ticks at all,
which is what a countdown that does not run during sleep would look like.

**It does not count down.** A later capture caught two ticks with the cycle 92 s after
the last one, and every tick carried the same value (`0x02C0` = 704). So the tick count
and the gap to the cycle both vary; only the two-minute spacing has held. The 13-seconds
figure from the first pass does not generalise.

**The `0x10xx` / `0xE065` shape fires on timer-driven cycles and never on commanded
ones.** `0x341064`+`0x341065` at 16:36:48, `0x34E065` at 20:49:38, `0x341064` at
23:48:34, `0x34E065` at 02:14:32 — four for four on automatic cycles, against none for
the cycle triggered by a written `0x02010201`, and none for the wake-released one. The
value alternates between the two forms with no visible trigger.

**`0x4F1065` fired as a cycle ended**, putting the same `0x1065` on both registers.
That is this issue's premise landing on a second register in one capture.

One caution against the obvious conclusion: `0x34=1064` marking automatic cycles and
`0x01=0201` marking commanded ones held for two cycles and then broke — a cycle at
21:27:04 carried the button code with nobody at the machine. Not writing that one up as
answered.

Encoding itself still open.

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-19:_

Reproduced independently, on a separate 3d22h capture (2026-08-15→19, two robots, ESP 1.1.75). The family is real and it is on both registers:

| register | values | emissions |
|---|---|---|
| `0x34` | `0x1064` ×25, `0x1065` ×6, `0x3065` ×2, `0x2064`, `0x2065`, `0x4065` | 36, in 33 seconds |
| `0x4F` | `0xC065`, `0xE065` | 2 |

Of the 35 seconds carrying any of them, **none carries both** — so whatever this is, the two registers are not emitting it together.

The part worth adding: the high nibble is 1–4 on `0x34` and C/E on `0x4F`, and `0xE065` is exactly the value in this repo's own long-standing open question about a pre-cycle marker that "alternates `0x10xx` vs `0xE065`". That question and this issue are the same puzzle observed on two registers, and nobody had connected them. Both are now filed together in `docs/devices/litter-robot-4/capture-notebook.md`.

On the timing decode: confirmed, with one correction. `0x34 = 0x02C0` fired **164 times** in this window, spacing exactly 120 s, and it is **always alone in its second** (164 of 164 — no other register, and no other `0x34` value). It fires in bursts of 1 to 15 ticks. But it isn't a countdown: the value never changes, so it marks the wait rather than counting it down, and the burst length and the gap to the cycle are both variable. Bursts of 15 mean half an hour of ticking, which the tick itself doesn't explain.

One methodological note that cost us a wrong number here, in case it's useful against your captures: collapsing a second into `{register: value}` is lossy, because a register can emit several distinct values in the same second. `0x4F` does it in 182 of 489 seconds and `0x34` in 69 of 335 — so a scalar map understates exactly the two registers this issue is about.

title: Protocol finding: 0xX06Y value family on BOTH 0x34 and 0x4F — a second activity encoding?

body:
_Recreated from GitHub issue [#7](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/issues/7), opened by @CryingPecan on 2026-08-08, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

---

Cross-robot evidence (one robot on whiskerless, one still on cloud for ground truth):

- Cloud robot: `optimalLitterLevel` = **450**, litterLevel 451-452 mm → litterLevelPercentage 0.9, state OPTIMAL
- Whiskerless robot: idles at **459-460 mm** at its own maintain target (LitterHopper, ~90% setting); whiskerless's absolute mm→% curve reads this as ~70%, while the cloud called the equivalent state 90%

So the cloud % is computed **relative to a per-robot optimal**, not from an absolute curve — no universal mm→% formula can be correct. Also confirmed directionality during a deliberate hopper run-dry: litterLevel mm RISES as litter drops (it's a distance measurement).

**The missing piece is where optimalLitterLevel lives locally.** It's not in the state document. Plan on our second robot's conversion day: a full safe-read register sweep on a robot whose optimal we know is exactly 450, hunting the register that holds it. Possibly related: activity reg 0x5E (fires at cycle start/end, value ÷4 ≈ litter mm at level attitude — see PR #2's phase notes).

comments.body:
_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-12:_

Confirmed from this side: `optimalLitterLevel` is not in the local state document. 69 distinct state fields across 50 hours on two robots, and `litterLevel` is the only litter-related one.

The approach here went sideways rather than hunting the anchor. Percentage is calibrated per robot now: one button press with the globe filled to the line pins it, otherwise it learns the extremes over time. That sidesteps the missing optimal instead of solving it.

A register sweep on the 450 robot is still the thing that would actually answer it.

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-16:_

The calibrated scale has now been checked against a human eye at the machine, on both
robots, from photographs taken at the same minute as the readings:

| Signal | Robot said | Eye said | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| waste drawer | `DFILevelPercent` 78 | ~78 % | accurate |
| globe litter | `litterLevel` ~445 | ~67 % | accurate |
| hopper | ~half | mostly full | **under-reports** |

So the missing anchor is not costing the globe percentage anything measurable. The one
signal that is out is the hopper gauge, and that is a learned-scale problem rather than
a decode problem — it has fewer extremes to learn from and had not yet seen a full one.

Two smaller corrections from the same session, both of which touch the calibrate-to-the-
line workflow: the globe **does** have a moulded fill line (this repo had stopped
claiming it for want of evidence, and it is there), and the filter has no date tab,
printed mark or indicator of any kind, with no register reporting its state either.

A register sweep on the 450 robot is still the thing that would answer the original
question rather than sidestep it.

title: Litter level %: the cloud's percent is relative to a per-robot optimalLitterLevel — the local mm→% curve can't match without that anchor

body:
_Recreated from GitHub issue [#8](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/issues/8), opened by @CryingPecan on 2026-08-08, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

---

Omnibus of activity registers we've observed consistently but can't fully decode yet. All evidence from continuous production capture on ESP 1.4.4 (+ owner-narrated sessions); raw logs available.

- **0x57 (hopper link) positive values**: every visit runs the ritual 30 → mid-value → 19. The -15 disconnect and the dispense-phase fill gauge are solved (PR #3), but what 30/19 are, and what the mid-value measures (it loosely tracks visit weight — hopper load-cell?), remain open.
- **0x6F**: fires once at visit end, values 5-2182. Tested and REJECTED: minutes-since-last-visit, 0x57 echo, visit duration. Open.
- **0xB9**: closes every visit with value 1 or 2; no clean correlation found with weight presence, duration, or which cat. (An early tare-context guess was falsified — both values occur on ordinary visits.)
- **0x67**: an indexed triple (0x01xx/0x02xx/0x03xx) once per cycle, small varying counts. Torque/pinch counters?
- **0x0B annunciator values 102/105** paired with constant `0x33 = 34` at irregular hours: 105 is proven to fire on a Reset press (tare context); 102 and the 0x33 pairing are open.
- **Boot burst** (captured via a power cycle): 0x7F announces board identity (values match mbHardware/mbBom/etc.), 0x7E×7 init ticks, then 0x73/0x74/0x75 — 0x74 carried 490/530/998, calibration constants? None of these ever appear outside the boot window.
- **0x56 (drawer bay) code variance**: removal is a stable 10 (2/2 narrated pulls); re-insert codes VARY (14, 28) and 12 fires occasionally with the drawer seated (PR #3 decodes 10-vs-anything-else defensively, but the actual code meanings are open).

comments.body:
_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-10:_

Update: the `0x0B` half of this is solved and shipped in `1f48c8d`.

`0x0B` is a status annunciator that fires alongside state transitions and names the event. Every value is now labelled against a live observed event:

| value | meaning |
|---|---|
| 7 | bonnet removed |
| 9 | cat detected |
| 12 | filter wizard waiting |
| 20 | cycle running |
| 22 | ready |
| 102 | night light transition |
| 105 | reset / tare |

The "random housekeeping chatter" was never random. 102 fires on dusk, dawn and room light changes, caught when the capture happened to be running while someone flipped a light switch; 105 fires on a Reset press, physical or written. Credit to @CryingPecan for the labelling work.

Also resolved from the wider register hunt since this issue was filed:

* **`0x01` is the panel button register and it accepts writes.** The value is `<button bitmask><press type>`. This is what unblocked every action command.
* **The readable register file is `0x00`-`0x7F`**, 123 of 128 addresses answering, with one contiguous gap at `0x6A`-`0x6E`. Nothing above `0x7F` answers a read. Reads must be paced ~3 s apart or the robot stops answering and you will wrongly conclude a register is unimplemented.
* **`0x1D` is a per-day bitmask**, not a boolean.
* **`0x56` reports that the waste drawer moved but not which way** — that one is documented as an open problem rather than solved, with what would settle it.

Still open here: `0x10`-`0x15` (live counters, values change between passes), `0x2C`, `0x2F`, `0x30`, `0x33`, `0x48`-`0x4A`, `0x50`-`0x55`, `0x5E`, `0x64`, `0x73`-`0x77`, `0x7B`. Leaving this issue open for those.

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-12:_

Two of these moved, and one of them cuts against what is written up here, which is the interesting part.

**`0x6F`**: listed above as tested and rejected for visit duration. On a 1.1.75 pair it matches the weight-on-scale span to within 3 seconds in 8 of 8, and is omitted on every visit under 15 seconds. Meanwhile `0xBC`, the one actually named `CAT_VISIT_DURATION`, matches no span that could be constructed.

**`0xB9`**: clean threshold here. `1` for all 8 closes with `0xBC <= 19`, `2` for all 8 with `0xBC >= 23`.

Before assuming either result is wrong: the two robots here turn out to differ in **mainboard** firmware, not just ESP. `mbRevision` 89 vs 93, `mbBuild` 1 vs 2, `mbRevisionId` 41027 vs 41088, with `espFirmware` identical at 1.1.75 on both. That would explain a lot of the cross-robot disagreements on both sides. What does the 1.4.4 robot report for `mbRevision` and `mbBuild`?

**`0x57` positives**: the 30 → mid → 19 ritual matches here exactly. Worth flagging though that the register is not the hopper link. Positives showed up with the hopper physically off the robot, and `-15` fires for just opening the hopper drawer.

`0x67` still open here too.

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-16:_

A narrated power cycle put a first observation on two registers from the still-open list
above, and settled a decode that had been recorded backwards.

**`0x50` and `0x7B` are power-transition registers.** A shutdown emits `0x04`, `0x06`,
`0x50`, `0x72`, `0x7B` and nothing else in the capture does, with `0x50` reading the same
148 on both edges. That does not name them, but it does take them out of the
idle-chatter pile.

**`robotStatus` 1 and 3 are the down-stroke; 2 is the up-stroke.** Run separately:

| | sequence | `0x31` unitPowerStatus |
|---|---|---|
| power **down** | `0x340001` → `0x340003` | 1 → **0** |
| power **up** | `0x340002` → ready (4) | 0 → **1** |

An earlier capture saw `1 → 3 → 2 → 13` across an off *and* an on and could not say
which half was which; this repo had 1 written up as `powering_up`, which was wrong.
`0x31` moves after all — it had looked static because a mains→battery swap leaves it
alone.

**`0x32` is the sleep flag**, driven by holding Cycle. An LR4 has no menu and cannot be
given a sleep *time* at the panel at all, which is worth knowing before designing a test
around one.

**The `0x56` seat-only asymmetry is dead.** One robot was silent on the pull and spoke
on the seat (`0x560017`); the other emitted `0x56000A` **both ways**, an hour later. Same
firmware family, opposite behaviour.

**`0x57` rides along on a waste-drawer pull too**, with a negative code that differs per
unit — **−30** on one, **−215** on the other. More evidence against it being the hopper
link, on top of the positives you saw with the hopper physically detached.

**`0x6F` and `0xBC` co-emit.** `registers.md` said the two had never been seen on the
same robot; they landed in the same second — `0x6F0029` (41) with `0xBC000A` (10) — and
`0x6F` was exact again, matching a 41 s `0x37` `0x11`→`0x10` occupancy span. Ninth of
nine. `0xBC` = 10 is not a rival reading of the same thing: 10 s of settled weight inside
41 s of occupancy fits both decodes, and `0xB9` came in at `1`, matching its documented
`<19 → 1` threshold.

Still open from the list above: `0x10`–`0x15`, `0x2C`, `0x2F`, `0x30`, `0x33`,
`0x48`–`0x4A`, `0x51`–`0x55`, `0x5E`, `0x64`, `0x67`, `0x73`–`0x77`.

Still curious what the 1.4.4 robot reports for `mbRevision` and `mbBuild` — the two
robots here differ in mainboard firmware while reporting identical `espFirmware`, which
would explain a good deal of the cross-robot disagreement on both sides.

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-19:_

A fresh 3d22h capture (2026-08-15→19, two robots) touches four of these.

**`0xB9` — there is a clean correlation, but not against the things you tried.** You tested weight presence, duration and which cat. Try it against `0xBC`: of the 41 seconds carrying both, the split is **41 of 41** — forty at `0xB9 = 1` with `0xBC` in 0–15, one at `0xB9 = 2` with `0xBC` far above.

And there's a likely reason it looked uncorrelated: **`0xBC` leads `0xB9` by 1–2 seconds.** 35 of the 76 seconds carrying either carry only one, so a same-second join drops 16 of 57 `0xB9` emissions (28%) and 19 of 60 `0xBC` (32%). Correlate over a small window, not a single second.

**Every out-of-range value we have is one Reset artifact — which may matter for your `0x6F` range.** We caught `0x6F = 24608` (6.8 h, far outside your 5–2182). It is not independent:

```
13:11:48  0x01=[0, 1025]          <- Reset press
13:11:53  0x09=2960  0x6F=24608
13:11:57  0xB9=2     0xBC=15699
```

Nine seconds on one robot, straight after a Reset. Since a Reset re-tares the scale (your own `0x0B = 105` = `reset_tare` finding), the reading is that the load-cell-derived registers emit garbage briefly afterwards rather than that several registers independently produce bad durations. **Worth excluding Reset-adjacent seconds before decoding `0x6F`, `0x09`, `0xB9` or `0xBC`** — it may tighten your 5–2182 range, and it's a caveat on our own `0xB9` result above, since the single high sample sits inside this episode.

**`0x74` is not a fixed constant, but two boots can't say more than that.** Two boot windows, one per robot: 13, 251, 256, 492, 555, 557, 768, 1010 — near your 490/530/998 without matching any. That rules out one burned-in value; per-robot, per-configuration and per-boot all still fit. Repeated boots of the *same* robot would separate them.

**Two codes for your lists:** `0x0B = 103` (once — you have 102/105) and `0x56 = 23` (once, against `10` ×4 — you have 10/12/14/28).

**On `0x6F` and visit duration** — you have it tested and rejected, our `registers.md` has it matching 9/9. I think that's a definitional mismatch rather than a disagreement: we match it against the **weight-on-scale span**, not total occupancy, and separately read `0xBC` as seconds of *settled* weight. If you rejected it against occupancy, both results can stand. Worth checking which quantity your rejection used.

Finally, `0x33` held **34 in all 55 readings**, both robots, four days — so the `0x0B`/`0x33` pairing you note is real (19 seconds carry both, `0x33` beside `0x0B` 102 most often) but `0x33` itself will not move under passive capture. It needs a deliberate perturbation.

title: Partially-decoded activity registers — open leads with 12 days of evidence

body:
_Recreated from GitHub pull request [#9](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/pull/9), opened by @CryingPecan on 2026-08-10, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

_This is a record of the pull request, not the pull request itself: its commits are kept in the maintainer's archive and were not pushed here._

---

You know that mqtt command we texted you tonight? Here it is grown up, with everything the narrated wizard run taught us. All from a physical run of Whisker's documented panel chord (long-press Cycle+Empty) on the 1.4.4, wire-captured end to end.

## The chord cracked the button encoding open

The combo emitted `0x010A02`: **hi byte = button bitmask, lo byte = press type**. Cycle 0x02 | Empty 0x08 = 0x0A (Empty's bit now proven), press type 02 = long press vs the 01 shorts we had. So `PANEL_BUTTON_FILTER_CHANGE = 0x0A02`, and the untested space is now legible: long-press Empty alone (0x0802) is presumably your missing empty cycle.

## The wizard, fully choreographed

- **robotStatus 14 = changing_filter** — the local int your string map was waiting for. Held for the wizard's entire life. Mapping it also routes the wizard through LITTER_UNRELIABLE_STATUSES, which matters: we captured 575 mm mid-wizard on a 458 mm fill.
- **cycleStatus 14 → 15**: rotating-to-park → parked-and-waiting. Waits indefinitely; bonnet off/on during the wait triggers nothing (0x3A flips + annunciation only).
- **Reset is the return trigger** — the globe rides the normal level/home rails home, status 14 throughout, then 4/ready. So your existing panel_reset button already completes the flow.
- **odometerFilterCycles counts wizard entries, stamped at chord time** (2→3 live). Not a countdown — the app's replace-filter nag must be cloud-computed. A local robot never nags.

## Bonus: the 0x0B annunciator is now a dictionary

Every value labeled against a live event: 7 bonnet, 9 cat, 12 wizard-waiting, 20 cycle, 22 ready, and the 'random housekeeping' pair from issue #8 solved — **102 = night-light transitions** (dusk, dawn, and light switches; caught when the owner flipped a room light with the capture running) and **105 = reset/tare**. Shipped as documentation-grade `STATUS_ANNUNCIATIONS`.

## The button

'Park for filter change' goes through your existing press machinery unchanged — motor-gated by value, at-most-once, echo-confirmed, with robotStatus-14 as the state fallback (the wizard's persistence makes it the best fallback of the three buttons).

**The honest caveat:** the physical chord is fully proven; the *synthesised* chord write is the one untested link — first press-type-02 write anyone will have sent. Same posture cycle/reset were in when you merged them off three trials. Both robots are standing by; first trial settles it.

134 tests pass, six new ones covering the chord command, the motor gate, wizard status/phase decode, and the mid-wizard litter suppression.

comments.body:
_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-10:_

Taking most of this. The chord capture is the piece that mattered: hi byte = button bitmask, lo byte = press type is the right reading, and it matches what I independently captured on the 1.1.75 (Power `0x0101`, Cycle `0x0201`, Reset `0x0401`, Empty `0x0801`). The `0x0B` annunciator dictionary is the best thing in the PR and closes #8. `robotStatus 14`, the wizard choreography, and the mid-wizard litter suppression are all going in.

The one thing that cannot ship is the button itself. You called the synthesised chord "the one untested link", so here is the test.

Three writes on 1.1.75, each with the activity stream captured end to end:

| written | robot answered | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `0x02010202` (Cycle long) | `0x010000` and nothing else | none |
| `0x02010402` (Reset long) | `0x010000` and nothing else | none, `nightLightMode` stayed 2 |
| `0x02010400` (Reset, press type `00`) | `0x010000`, then `0x010401`, `0x350000`, `0x0B0069` | a real Reset happened |

For comparison, a physical 3 second hold of Cycle emits `0x010202` on its own and the robot acts on it.

So an *unknown* press type (`00`) gets normalised to a short press and performed, while `02` produces no event at all. That is the shape of a value that is recognised and declined, not one falling through a default. The firmware performs short presses over MQTT and refuses long ones.

Independent corroboration, which I went looking for afterwards: pylitterbot's complete `LitterRobot4Command` list is 15 verbs, none of them a hold, and the one button verb is named `shortResetPress`. Whisker's own cloud has no long press either. It reaches the hold-only functions by writing the underlying setting instead, which is exactly what we already do for lockout (`0x17`), night light (`0x18`) and clump time (`0x16`).

That leaves the filter wizard genuinely unreachable from MQTT, because it is the one hold-only function with no backing settings register. Worth knowing rather than worth another trial.

Two smaller corrections while I am here:

* Empty alone is a **short** press, `0x0801`, not `0x0802`. Captured live, and `0x02010801` runs an empty cycle.
* Your `filter_change()` is classified `MOTOR`; our guard classifies panel button writes by value, and anything outside the proven set defaults to `DANGEROUS`. Moot now that the command is coming out, but noting it so the next command you add lands in the right bucket.

Your work is going into main as your commits, same as before. I will link them here when they land, then close this out.

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-10:_

Merged as `1f48c8d`, authored to you, now on main and mirrored here.

What went in:

* `robotStatus 14` and both wizard cycle phases (`filter_park` / `filter_wait`), with the wizard routed through the litter-suppression set. Your 575 mm reading on a 458 mm fill is exactly why that matters.
* `ODOMETER_FILTER_CYCLES` documented as counting wizard *entries* rather than being a countdown, which explains why a local robot never nags.
* `STATUS_ANNUNCIATIONS`, the whole dictionary. This is the best thing in the PR and it closes #8.
* The button bitmask / press type structure, which matched my independent capture on 1.1.75.

What did not, and why, in full detail in my earlier comment: the synthesised chord `0x02010A02`. Press type `02` is declined on the write path across three trials, and an unknown type (`00`) is normalised to a short press and performed, so it is a deliberate refusal rather than an unimplemented case. pylitterbot's LR4 verb list has no hold command either and names its one button verb `shortResetPress`, so Whisker's own cloud cannot do it. The filter wizard is the one hold-only function with no backing settings register, which makes it genuinely unreachable over MQTT.

Two corrections carried into the docs: Empty alone is a short press (`0x0801`, now shipped as a disabled-by-default button), and the `MOTOR` hazard class is gone entirely. That last one came out of this PR indirectly. Arguing about whether your chord should be `MOTOR` or `DANGEROUS` made it obvious the class was never doing any work, since writing `0x01` reproduces the exact code the panel emits and every caller passed `allow_motor=True` unconditionally anyway.

Thanks for the capture work. Closing this one since the commit is in.

title: feat(lr4): filter-change wizard decoded end to end + a button to start it

body:
_Recreated from GitHub pull request [#10](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/pull/10), opened by @CryingPecan on 2026-08-15, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

_This is a record of the pull request, not the pull request itself: its commits are kept in the maintainer's archive and were not pushed here._

---

## The field incident that motivated this

Converting our second robot (LR4S1232338, ESP 1.4.4) to whiskerless today, provisioning reported success end-to-end — DEVICE_ID_SET, WiFi apply, cert write, APPLY_CONFIG, reboot, all clean. The robot then vanished: off the Whisker cloud (so the config *took*), never on WiFi, never on the broker. It looked exactly like the permanent-MQTT-death failure mode, and we spent half an hour on broker listeners, firewall rules, and stale UniFi client entries before finding the real cause: **one mistyped character in the WiFi password at the blind `getpass` prompt**. Re-provisioning with the right password had the robot on EMQX 30 seconds after reboot.

The provisioner can't see a bad password today — the WiFi finalize is a fixed 12 s `sleep` and nothing checks the outcome. But the robot knows, and will say so if asked.

## What this does

`prov-config` is stock esp-idf WiFi provisioning, and the stock protocol includes `CmdGetStatus`, which the codec never sent. After SetConfig+Apply, we now poll it (1.5 s cadence, 20 s ceiling) instead of sleeping blind:

- **Connected** → prints `WiFi connected (ip=192.168.2.41)` and proceeds early (a beat of settle first — got-IP is what finalizes the provisioning state machine, and the old 12 s was really standing in for that). You also get the robot's fresh IP for free, which is exactly what you want next anyway.
- **ConnectionFailed / AuthError** → raises `WiFi join failed: authentication failed — almost always a mistyped WiFi password`, **before the endpoint/cert writes**, so the broker config is untouched and the remedy is just re-running provision.
- **ConnectionFailed / NetworkNotFound** → same, naming the SSID.
- **No answer** (firmware without GetStatus, GATT hiccups) → degrades to the old behavior: run out the window, warn `verify the robot actually appears on your network`, continue. A silent firmware can't fail a good join.

## Wire model (the two proto3 gotchas)

- `fail_reason` `AuthError` is enum value **0**, but it's a oneof arm, so protobuf-c emits the field anyway — presence is explicit. The tests pin this exact encoding (`0x50 0x00`).
- `sta_state` `Connected` is **also** 0 — a plain field, so proto3 keeps it *off* the wire, making a bare `RespGetStatus` ambiguous. Success is therefore only ever read from the `WifiConnectedState` oneof arm (which esp-idf always populates, with `ip4_addr`), never inferred from an absent `sta_state`.

## Caveat, flagged like last time

The builders/parsers match the stock esp-idf `wifi_config.proto` byte-for-byte and are fully unit-tested (13 new tests: wire fixtures both directions, plus the verify loop against a fake transport — auth failure raises, connected returns, silent firmware falls through). But **the GetStatus round-trip has not yet been exercised against a live robot** — both of ours are now provisioned and happy, and I didn't re-provision one just to watch it succeed. It's a read-only query, so the safe live check is: pairing mode → connect → GetStatus, no writes. First re-provision by whoever gets there first; happy to run it on our hardware next time either robot needs a BLE touch.

Note: `tests/test_link.py` / `tests/test_mqtt.py` have 15 failures on current `main` in my local py3.12 env, pre-existing and untouched by this branch (565 → 578 passing).

body:
_Recreated from GitHub pull request [#11](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/pull/11), opened by @CryingPecan on 2026-08-18, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

_This is a record of the pull request, not the pull request itself: its commits are kept in the maintainer's archive and were not pushed here._

---

## The bug

`_apply_activity` counts a dispense only when **more than one** `HopperDispensed` event arrives **in a single activity message**. On ESP 1.4.4 that never happens: every real dispense is published as **three separate single-reading activity messages** — the phase-0 step marker first, then the phase-1 fill gauge and phase-2 marker ~20 s later (the last two ~0.1 s apart).

Verified on 5 dispenses across our two 1.4.4 robots in the 24/7 raw capture. The shape is completely consistent; a one-message triple has never been observed on this firmware:

```
robot A  04:47:05  0x0C010A      robot B  17:52:04  0x0C0114
         04:47:15  0x0C1057               17:52:24  0x0C1041
         04:47:15  0x0C2078               17:52:24  0x0C2079
```

Consequences on 1.4.4:
- **Fresh install with a hopper: the capability is never sighted**, so all five hopper entities sit `disabled_by: integration` forever. Our robot B was converted 3 days ago, dispensed the next day, and has `hopper_seen` absent and everything disabled.
- **Existing installs only keep hopper entities via RESTORED/LEGACY evidence**, and go stale: robot A's `last_hopper_dispensed` is frozen at its last pre-rc.9 dispense while the wire shows two dispenses since. Every fill-gauge sample is discarded, so the learned hopper scale never advances either.

## The fix

The burst is now assembled **across messages**: each `HopperDispensed` reading is folded into a small `pending_dispense` {phase: value} buffer on `DerivedState` (serialized, so a consumer reload mid-burst doesn't lose it), and the dispense is believed once **two distinct phases** land inside a 60 s window.

The false positive the old gate guarded against — a type-1 diagnostic READ of 0x0C decoding to a single `HopperDispensed` — stays rejected, and I think the distinct-phase rule is actually a stronger form of the guard: reads return whatever the register last held, so repeated polls produce the *same* phase every time and can never assemble a two-phase burst, no matter how close together they land. (The old gate would have accepted two identical-phase readings in one message.)

One-message bursts (1.1.75) prove on the same message exactly as before — the existing tests and the integration triples pass unchanged.

## Tests

- split-across-messages burst proves the hopper and applies the fill gauge (the real 1.4.4 timing)
- repeated same-phase reads inside the window prove nothing
- two lone reads farther apart than the window prove nothing
- a burst interrupted by a consumer reload between phases still proves (round-trips through `as_dict`)

74/74 in `test_derive.py` + `test_events.py`; full suite green except the 15 pre-existing `test_link`/`test_mqtt` failures in my local py3.12 env (same ones as before, unrelated).

Caveat: window is 60 s on the strength of the captured ~20 s gap; if 1.1.75 ever splits a burst wider than that we'd miss it, but no such capture exists.

comments.body:
_@CryingPecan on GitHub, 2026-08-18:_

Two live corroborations since filing, from tonight's captures (both robots ESP 1.4.4):

1. **Two more dispenses, same three-message shape** (6th and 7th observed) — including one from a hopper that turned out to be physically **empty** (owner-confirmed): the auger ran on schedule and the phase-1 gauge flatlined at 64–65, the bare-auger empty-floor signature. That's a concrete picture of what this gate costs today: with the fill samples discarded, `hopper_out_of_litter` can never learn the floor, so an empty hopper goes unnoticed until someone looks inside.

2. **The ~20 s gap has an official explanation.** Whisker's LitterHopper docs state the auger runs *up to 20 seconds* per dispense, and the docs also describe the below-optimal decision being taken at cycle end with the dispense executing during the *next* cycle. The phase-0 → phase-1 gap matches the documented auger runtime exactly — so the split isn't publish jitter, it's the hardware: phase 0 marks auger start and the fill gauge reports after it stops. The 60 s window bounds a documented 20 s mechanism with margin (pushed a comment update to the branch saying so).

Related find while watching this robot, separate from this PR: the panel litter-level recalibration combo (long-press Cycle+Reset+Empty) echoed as `0x010E02` — the OR'd-bitmask press model holding up on a three-button chord — and register `0x69` read back as the stored optimal litter bed level on both our units (458 / 460, matching each unit's maintained level; the cloud doc's `optimalLitterLevel` was 450 on the unit before its anchor was reset). Annunciation 105 fired on that combo too, which would explain why nine plain Reset presses never raised it. Happy to write that up properly as a docs PR if useful.

_@CryingPecan on GitHub, 2026-08-18:_

On the CI failure: `Shell scripts and documentation links` failed with `FAIL 403 https://www.litter-robot.com/support/article/litter-robot-4-control-panel-button-functions/` — that's the external-citation check, not this change (no links added; the citation predates the branch, behind docs/devices/litter-robot-4/control-panel.md).

The page is alive: from a residential IP it returns 200 with both a browser UA *and* the script's own `whiskerless-ci` UA. So Whisker's WAF is blocking by IP reputation (GitHub's runner ranges), not by user-agent — which means a UA tweak in `packaging/check-external-links.sh` likely won't help, and this will flake for every PR until the WAF changes its mind or the script does. One option: treat 403 as "resolves" for this URL — for citation-rot purposes a WAF challenge still proves the path routes to something Whisker actively defends, and the failure mode the check exists for (article moved/deleted) shows up as 404/410, not 403.

All other jobs green (both platforms, both float/floor, integration, hassfest).

_@SisyphusMD on GitHub, 2026-08-18:_

Landed as `f28dc6a` on the Forgejo source, with you as the commit author — it will
appear here on the next mirror push. Thank you, this was a good catch and a well
argued one; the evidence in the description is what made it reviewable.

Five changes on the way in:

**The firmware framing was too narrow.** The description has 1.1.75 packing the
burst into one message and only 1.4.4 splitting it. Our own capture notebook has
robot 2 — an ESP **1.1.75** unit — splitting it too, phase-0 about twenty seconds
ahead of the phase-1/2 pair, and robot 1 has never dispensed at all. So a
one-message burst has never actually been observed on any robot, on either
firmware. That makes the fix a stronger statement than the PR claimed: the old
gate did not fail on one firmware, it required a shape the wire has never sent.
The constant's comment, the code comment and the commit message now say that.

**The burst is spent when it proves.** It stayed populated, so the trailing
phase-2 marker re-entered the proof arm moments later and moved
`last_hopper_dispensed` again for a dispense already counted. Cleared on proof
now. (I also tried refusing any burst re-assembling inside `DISPENSE_DEDUPE`,
which is wrong — two real dispenses can arrive close together and each gauge is
worth recording. `tests/integration/test_hopper_detection.py` catches that, and
did.)

**Restored phases are bounds-checked.** `from_dict` accepted any integer, but the
wire splits one 16-bit reading into a 4-bit phase and a 12-bit value. A stored
impossible phase would have counted toward the two-phase proof and let a single
later register read look like a dispense.

**The reload test claimed more than it delivers.** The library does round-trip a
half-assembled burst, but the coordinator writes the derived snapshot only when a
sighting fires, and a first phase fires nothing — so Home Assistant restarting
inside the ~20 s gap does lose that one dispense, and the next one proves it. The
test now says exactly that instead of implying HA survives it.

**Coverage.** The defensive parse was two uncovered statements; there is a test
for it now, plus one for a burst whose middle gauge message is lost, which is a
real case on a lossy link. `derive.py` is back to 100%.

Also added the CHANGELOG entry and a note on backlog #68 — if every fill sample
was being discarded, the learned hopper scale was starved, which may well be the
whole of that under-reporting. Worth a fresh measurement before chasing the span.

body:
_Recreated from GitHub issue [#13](https://github.com/SisyphusMD/whiskerless/issues/13), opened by @b12e on 2026-10-28, when the GitHub copy became read-only._

---

### whiskerless version

0.2.0-rc.69 (HA core 2026.11.0b0, HA OS 18.2)

### Which part?

Home Assistant integration

### Robot firmware version

N/A

### What happened?

After updating to HA 2026.11.0b0, the config entry fails to set up:

```
File "/config/custom_components/whiskerless/__init__.py", line 553, in async_setup_entry
    _recheck_sightings(hass, entry)
File "/config/custom_components/whiskerless/__init__.py", line 234, in _recheck_sightings
    last_states = restore_state.async_get(hass).last_states
AttributeError: 'RestoreStateData' object has no attribute 'last_states'
```

### Cause

HA 2026.11 removed `RestoreStateData.last_states`. Stored states are now split into `last_states_by_entity_id` (entities without a registry entry) and `last_states_by_entity_registry_id` (keyed by registry id), and read through a new `async_get_stored_state(entity_id)`. That getter also follows entity_id renames, because the registry id survives a rename. 2026.10.x and older only have `last_states`.

The integration reads `last_states` directly in five places:

- `__init__.py`: `_seed_missing_gauge`, `_recheck_sightings` (passed on to `_reproved`), and `_rename_entities`, which moves the cache entry across a rename
- `coordinator.py`: the restored binary sensor lookup

### Suggested fix

A small compat module that uses `async_get_stored_state` when it exists and falls back to `last_states` otherwise, so the 2025.3 minimum in hacs.json keeps working. The manual cache move on rename is skipped on 2026.11, since core now handles that. I'm running this patch locally on 2026.11.0b0: the entry loads and restored states (e.g. the clean cycle button's last press) come back. I did not run the test suite.

<details>
<summary>Patch</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/custom_components/whiskerless/__init__.py b/custom_components/whiskerless/__init__.py
index 6d2cb7c..e129d76 100644
--- a/custom_components/whiskerless/__init__.py
+++ b/custom_components/whiskerless/__init__.py
@@ -3,7 +3,7 @@
 from __future__ import annotations
 
 import re
-from collections.abc import Mapping
+from collections.abc import Callable
 from typing import Any
 
 from awesomeversion import AwesomeVersion
@@ -28,6 +28,7 @@ from .const import (
     LOGGER,
 )
 from .coordinator import SIGHTING_OPTIONS, WhiskerlessConfigEntry, WhiskerlessCoordinator
+from .restore_compat import move_stored_state, stored_state
 
 # Option key recording which version last swept the entity registry.
 _SWEPT_BY = "retired_entities_swept_by"
@@ -194,7 +195,7 @@ def _seed_missing_gauge(hass: HomeAssistant, entry: WhiskerlessConfigEntry) -> N
     entity_id = registry.async_get_entity_id(
         domain, DOMAIN, f"{entry.data[CONF_SERIAL]}_{key}"
     )
-    stored = restore_state.async_get(hass).last_states.get(entity_id) if entity_id else None
+    stored = stored_state(hass, entity_id)
     if stored is None:
         return
     extra = stored.extra_data.as_dict() if stored.extra_data else {}
@@ -231,7 +232,6 @@ def _recheck_sightings(hass: HomeAssistant, entry: WhiskerlessConfigEntry) -> No
     the rules may revert that.
     """
     registry = er.async_get(hass)
-    last_states = restore_state.async_get(hass).last_states
     # From entry data, not runtime_data: this runs BEFORE the coordinator is
     # built, so the coordinator reads the post-sweep flags and a re-proving
     # report can re-sight in the same session.
@@ -267,7 +267,7 @@ def _recheck_sightings(hass: HomeAssistant, entry: WhiskerlessConfigEntry) -> No
         # evidence table's call: a restored visit duration is not, because the
         # builds that recorded one did so from evidence since proven wrong.
         if derive.sighting_stands(capability, Evidence.RESTORED) and _reproved(
-            capability, serial, registry, last_states, options
+            capability, serial, registry, lambda eid: stored_state(hass, eid), options
         ):
             options[seen_key] = str(Evidence.RESTORED)
             continue
@@ -291,7 +291,7 @@ def _reproved(
     capability: Capability,
     serial: str,
     registry: er.EntityRegistry,
-    last_states: Mapping[str, restore_state.StoredState],
+    lookup: Callable[[str | None], restore_state.StoredState | None],
     options: dict[str, Any],
 ) -> bool:
     """Whether this capability's own past reports still prove it."""
@@ -301,7 +301,7 @@ def _reproved(
         return True
     for domain, key in _RESTORE_PROOF.get(capability, ()):
         entity_id = registry.async_get_entity_id(domain, DOMAIN, f"{serial}_{key}")
-        stored = last_states.get(entity_id) if entity_id else None
+        stored = lookup(entity_id)
         if stored is None:
             continue
         # A sensor unavailable at the last shutdown still carries its real
@@ -472,9 +472,7 @@ def _rename_entities(hass: HomeAssistant, entry: WhiskerlessConfigEntry) -> None
         # comes back `unknown` after the rename: a button forgets when it was
         # last pressed, and the hopper gauge forgets a reading the detection
         # sweep reads as proof the hardware exists.
-        cached = restore_state.async_get(hass).last_states
-        if entity_id in cached:
-            cached[target] = cached.pop(entity_id)
+        move_stored_state(hass, entity_id, target)
         LOGGER.warning(
             "Renamed %s to %s — update any automation or dashboard that used the old id",
             entity_id,
diff --git a/custom_components/whiskerless/coordinator.py b/custom_components/whiskerless/coordinator.py
index 1e24124..f5bc22e 100644
--- a/custom_components/whiskerless/coordinator.py
+++ b/custom_components/whiskerless/coordinator.py
@@ -23,7 +23,6 @@ from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant, callback
 from homeassistant.exceptions import ConfigEntryNotReady, HomeAssistantError
 from homeassistant.helpers import device_registry as dr
 from homeassistant.helpers import entity_registry as er
-from homeassistant.helpers import restore_state
 from homeassistant.helpers.update_coordinator import DataUpdateCoordinator, UpdateFailed
 from homeassistant.util import dt as dt_util
 
@@ -73,6 +72,7 @@ from .const import (
     HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL,
     LOGGER,
 )
+from .restore_compat import stored_state
 
 #: Which config-entry option records each capability's first sighting. The
 #: library decides what counts as proof; Home Assistant decides where it is kept.
@@ -200,7 +200,7 @@ class WhiskerlessCoordinator(DataUpdateCoordinator[WhiskerlessData]):
         entity_id = registry.async_get_entity_id(
             Platform.BINARY_SENSOR, DOMAIN, f"{self.serial}_{key}"
         )

+"""Read the restore-state cache on both sides of the 2026.11 change.
+
+Home Assistant 2026.11 replaced RestoreStateData.last_states (keyed by
+entity_id) with two maps, one keyed by entity registry id, and a getter that
+also follows entity_id renames. Older releases only have the dict.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant
+from homeassistant.helpers import restore_state
+
+
+def stored_state(hass: HomeAssistant, entity_id: str | None) -> restore_state.StoredState | None:
+    """The cached state of entity_id, if the restore cache has one."""
+    if not entity_id:
+        return None
+    data = restore_state.async_get(hass)
+    if (getter := getattr(data, "async_get_stored_state", None)) is not None:
+        return getter(entity_id)
+    return data.last_states.get(entity_id)
+
+
+def move_stored_state(hass: HomeAssistant, old: str, new: str) -> None:
+    """Carry a cached state across an entity_id rename.
+
+    Only needed before 2026.11: since then the cache is keyed by registry id,
+    which a rename keeps, and the getter rewrites the stored entity_id.
+    """
+    data = restore_state.async_get(hass)
+    cached = getattr(data, "last_states", None)
+    if cached is not None and old in cached:
+        cached[new] = cached.pop(old)
```
